caseStudies.overview: A dual-view molecular learning project that aligns graph and SELFIES representations for cross-modal retrieval and molecular generation.
caseStudies.problem: Molecules can be represented as both molecular graphs and token sequences. This project explores how to align those two views so they can support retrieval as well as generation.
caseStudies.approach: The notebook preprocesses molecules with RDKit, encodes graph and SELFIES views with separate neural branches, and trains them with contrastive alignment. Retrieval and generation are evaluated separately; generation uses top-k and nucleus sampling.

architecture.detail: RDKit preprocessing supplies a molecular graph and a SELFIES sequence for each molecule.
A residual graph convolutional network encodes graph structure while a causal Transformer encodes the SELFIES sequence.
The graph and sequence representations are jointly aligned for cross-modal retrieval.
The learned representations support bidirectional retrieval; the sequence model generates molecules with top-k or nucleus sampling.

caseStudies.resultSummary: The repository README reports retrieval, RDKit validity, and generation acceptance results for the project evaluation.
limitations: The README reports results for this project evaluation; it does not report experimental synthesis or downstream drug-development validation.
Generation acceptance and chemical validity do not establish the biological activity or safety of generated molecules.

caseStudies.overview: A graduate machine-learning project comparing kernel and non-kernel methods across four datasets with different data and scale challenges.
caseStudies.problem: The selected datasets bring different challenges, including missing values, outliers, class imbalance, nonlinear structure, and large-scale data. The project studies how those conditions affect model choice and analysis.
caseStudies.approach: Dataset-specific notebooks cover data cleaning and feature engineering, then compare methods such as linear and logistic models, K-nearest neighbors, decision trees, kernel SVM, kernel ridge regression, kernel KNN, and kernel PCA. The repository also documents failure, bias, and computational-complexity analysis.

architecture.detail: Separate notebooks cover Airbnb Open Data, NYC 311 service requests, IBM HR employee attrition, and online retail transactions.
The workflows examine cleaning, feature engineering, missing data, outliers, and class imbalance.
Kernel methods are compared with listed non-kernel approaches, including linear/logistic models, KNN, and decision trees.
The project topics include failure and bias analysis as well as computational complexity.

caseStudies.resultSummary: The public notebooks and expanded report present dataset-specific analyses and charts. The README does not state one aggregate score or a universal winning method.
limitations: Conclusions are scoped to the four datasets and tasks in the repository; they should not be read as a universal ranking of kernel and non-kernel methods.
The README presents no single cross-dataset metric that summarizes the comparisons.

caseStudies.overview: From-scratch Hough Transform implementations applied to traffic-light detection, lane detection, and object localization.
caseStudies.problem: The project applies geometric voting methods to practical image-processing tasks: finding traffic-light circles and states, detecting lane lines, and localizing objects with a generalized transform.
caseStudies.approach: The repository describes Gaussian filtering and Sobel edge detection before Hough circle or line voting. Its generalized Hough work uses gradient-based voting and R-table construction; the algorithms are implemented mostly from scratch with NumPy and fundamental image-processing operations.

architecture.detail: Gaussian filtering and Sobel edge detection prepare image features for geometric voting.
Hough circles support lamp detection and state classification; the polar Hough line transform supports lane detection.
Gradient-based voting and an R-table support generalized Hough object localization.
The repository lists NumPy vectorization and OpenCV alongside its from-scratch transform implementations.

caseStudies.resultSummary: Repository outputs show a traffic-light example with detected lamp circles and state labels. The README describes the lane-detection and generalized-object tasks but gives no aggregate performance score.
limitations: The README does not publish quantitative accuracy or runtime results for the example tasks.
The visible overlay documents an example output; it does not establish performance across broader traffic or road conditions.

caseStudies.overview: An imbalanced-classification study comparing ensemble approaches for predicting severe COVID-19 cases from clinical and demographic data.
caseStudies.problem: The repository dataset has 1,585 samples, including 100 severe and 1,485 non-severe cases, an approximate 15:1 imbalance. The project focuses on evaluating the minority severe class under that skew.
caseStudies.approach: The repository compares a Hellinger Distance Decision Tree, bagging with majority-class undersampling, and AdaBoost.M1 with SMOTE. It lists missing-value imputation and feature selection and evaluates imbalance-aware measures including minority-class recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and G-mean.

architecture.detail: The README describes 40 input features across 1,585 samples, with 100 severe cases.
The project topics include missing-value imputation and feature selection.
Three listed approaches are HDDT, majority-class undersampling with bagging, and AdaBoost.M1 with SMOTE.
The repository lists minority-class recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and G-mean as evaluation measures.

caseStudies.resultSummary: The saved AdaBoost + SMOTE figure plots mean train error, test error, and severe-class F1 across boosting rounds, averaged over 10 runs. The README does not summarize one consolidated best score.
limitations: The documented dataset contains 100 severe cases, so the minority-class sample count is limited in the repository evaluation.
The README does not report external validation or a deployment study; results should be read as dataset-level experiments.
